description: deixis-codec-v1 linked form (dxl1) and the bridge — batch 1. Chunk octets hand-assembled from docs/CODEC.md §6; the SHA-256 digests are the one part of this corpus no reader can check by eye, so every digest carries its PREIMAGE as hex beside it and a replayer MUST recompute rather than trust. Bridge cases reference their flat counterpart BY NAME (CODEC-PLAN.md ruling 1) — the harness resolves names corpus-wide and fails loudly on a dangling one.
status: HISTORICAL: the withdrawn deixis-codec-v1 candidate (ADR 0011 §5), specified by docs/CODEC-v1.md; kept as its evidence, not rewritten. As authored: DRAFT — batch 1, authored against a CANDIDATE CONTRACT. Not frozen.

header.derivation: "dxl1" = 64 78 6c 31 · cuvarint(len(id)) = 02 · id = 00 01. Note the third octet differs from the flat header by one bit-pattern (66 → 6c): the two magics are one suite and move together (§16), and nothing here may be read as licensing a per-form version.

chunks.name: chunk/leaf-01
chunks.note: A leaf chunk: header, cuvarint(0) for an empty links header, then the body 00 01 01. A leaf has no children, so nlinks is 0 and the links header occupies exactly one octet — not zero.
pins: 1. The magic is exactly `"dxl1"`.
- v1 pins **SHA-256**. Hash agility is a new codec version, never a parameter.

The magic and
  the `id` are therefore *inside* the hashed octets:

chunk  := "dxl1" ‖ cuvarint(len(id)) ‖ id
        ‖ cuvarint(nlinks) ‖ hash{32}*                 # ← the LINKS HEADER

`uvarint` is unsigned LEB128: seven bits per octet, least-significant group first,
the high bit of each octet set on all but the last.
A leaf chunk has `nlinks = 0`. **One node, one chunk**

id := 0x00 ‖ cuvarint(n)              # PUBLIC — registry-assigned, n ≥ 1
    | 0x01 ‖ ns{16} ‖ cuvarint(k)     # PRIVATE / EXPERIMENTAL — self-scoped
- Total length is 2..32 octets; outside that range the artifact is **invalid**.
- `e : T → Bytes` — total, computable, and **lawful**: `x ≈ y ⟺ e(x) = e(y)`.
under SHA-256 collision resistance**.

chunks.name: chunk/inner-struct
chunks.note: Struct{62 ↦ Leaf(01)}: nlinks 01, one 32-octet hash (chunk/leaf-01's), then body 01 01 | 01 62 | 00 — the lentry ends in a LINK INDEX, never a raw hash. That is §6's rule that a body MUST NOT contain a hash, and it is what makes the links header the sole place a child is named.
pins:
Each hash in the links header is the SHA-256 (§7) of the referenced child's **entire
chunk octets** under this same layout.

Bodies reference children only by index into
that header; a body MUST NOT contain a raw hash.

chunk  := "dxl1" ‖ cuvarint(len(id)) ‖ id
        ‖ cuvarint(nlinks) ‖ hash{32}*                 # ← the LINKS HEADER
lentry := cuvarint(len(key)) ‖ key ‖ cuvarint(link-index)
2. `nlinks` equals the number of hashes present.
7. Key ordering, tag, count, payload and trailing rules are as in §5.

chunks.name: chunk/root-shared
chunks.note: THE POSITIVE SHARING CASE (law 2). Two identical subtrees under keys 61 and 63: the chunk is emitted ONCE, its hash listed ONCE in the header, and referenced TWICE from the body — both lentries carry link-index 00. First-use order is trivial here (one distinct child), and that is a LIMIT of this case rather than a design: a one-element header has exactly one order, so §6's first-use rule cannot be violated here and this case pins WHICH chunks without pinning IN WHAT ORDER the header names them. The author placed the multi-child case in batch 2; the codec lane overturned that on 2026-08-30 — see linked/first-use-order, which is its lawful twin and CAN fail. A core that emits the chunk twice produces a different closure for the same value and passes every other case in this corpus — which is why the invalid direction (duplicate_link_hash) does not cover this and never could.

cases.name: linked/first-use-order

discriminates.against: a core that SORTS the links header by hash instead of listing hashes in first-use order
discriminates.why: The two hashes are in OPPOSITE relative order under the two rules: first-use gives a07bb26f… then 0fcf34e8…, while sorting by hash gives 0fcf34e8… first. A hash-sorting encoder therefore emits different octets and a DIFFERENT ADDRESS for this value — recomputed here so the discrimination is checkable rather than asserted. The counterfactual is NOT a case: its refusal (links_out_of_order) is BATCH 2's, and this is its lawful twin. (This note said batch 3 until 2026-09-03 — a filing error of mine, made in both batch-1 files at once. Batch 3 is fault PRECEDENCE; a plain code belongs in batch 2.) ⛔ AND THE COUNTERFACTUAL HOLDS THE VALUE FIXED, WHICH IS THE WHOLE POINT AND IS ONE EDIT AWAY FROM BEING LOST: swapping the header order forces the body's LINK INDICES TO BE RENUMBERED, because an index is a position INTO that header. The counterfactual above carries 61 ↦ index 1 and 63 ↦ index 0. Swapping the header and LEAVING the indices alone yields 740c856eb14b285bddff51a67dbf2db8dada12d5ed7bb5a5acf6f7000574ec2f — which encodes 61 ↦ Leaf(02) and 63 ↦ Leaf(01), i.e. A DIFFERENT VALUE. That digest would still differ from the lawful address, so the case would appear to discriminate while proving nothing: two values SHOULD have two addresses. A counterfactual that changes the value is not a counterfactual. Recorded here because a later editor regenerating this digest has a one-line way to get it wrong and no tell.

cases.note: ⛔ THIS CASE EXISTS BECAUSE linked/sharing-is-lawful CANNOT FAIL ON ORDER. That case has nlinks=1, and a one-element header has exactly one order, so §6's first-use rule is unexercisable there — it pins WHICH chunks and not IN WHAT ORDER the header names them, which are the two halves of law 2's determinism. A case that cannot fail is not evidence about the rule it names. (Ruled by the codec lane, 2026-08-30, against the author's own placement of this case in batch 2.)

cases.name: address/flat-digest-is-not-an-address
cases.note: ONE value, TWO digests, and they are not interchangeable. The left is SHA-256 over the flat artifact's octets; the right is the value's ADDRESS — the linked ROOT hash, and nothing else (§7). Conflating them is the named failure the three-notion clause exists to prevent, and this is the only place a corpus can catch it: every other case would pass a core that quietly used the flat digest as an address. The address is spelled VERSION-QUALIFIED as (dxl1, digest) per ruling 2 — a bare 32 octets is not an address, and a corpus that spells it bare teaches the habit it should be refusing.
pins:
- **The content address of a value is the SHA-256 of its linked-form root chunk, and
  nothing else, ever.**

One value under two leaf codecs has two

under SHA-256 collision resistance**.

method.octets: Hand-assembled from CODEC.md §6, never emitted by an implementation.
method.digests: SHA-256, computed with a tool because no reader computes one by hand. Each is published WITH its preimage (`bytes`), so the corpus is checkable rather than trusted: recompute, do not accept. A digest whose preimage is absent is an assertion; one whose preimage is present is evidence.
method.verification: Every chunk's octets were parsed back through a reader written from the grammar — header, links header, body, link indices in range, no trailing bytes — and each digest recomputed from the published preimage.

Batch 3 is fault PRECEDENCE: one case per row of §10, with BOTH conditions genuinely observable — the leaf-holding/leaf-blind pair on the non_canonical_payload cases is already flagged there.

invalid_cases.name: invalid/bad-link-index
invalid_cases.note: nlinks 01 with ONE hash listed, and the lentry carries index 01 — one past the end. The header is well formed and the body's key ordering is fine, so every check except the range check passes. ⚠ A decoder that indexes without bounds-checking reads whatever follows the header in memory, so the failure direction is worse than a wrong value.

invalid_cases.name: invalid/unused-link
invalid_cases.clause: §6 rule 5 — every listed hash MUST be referenced by at least one lentry.
invalid_cases.note: Two hashes listed, ONE entry, referencing index 0 — so chunk/leaf-02's hash is listed and never used. Nothing is missing and nothing is out of range; the closure simply carries a chunk the value does not need. ⇒ This is the rule that makes the links header a FUNCTION of the value rather than a superset of it: without it, one value would have unboundedly many valid spellings and therefore unboundedly many addresses.

invalid_cases.name: invalid/duplicate-link-hash
invalid_cases.clause: §6 rule 3 — the same hash MUST NOT appear twice.
invalid_cases.note: chunk/leaf-01's hash listed at BOTH index 0 and index 1, with entries 61 and 63 pointing at one each. Both indices are in range and both hashes are referenced, so rules 4 and 5 pass — only rule 3 fires. ⭐ Its LAWFUL twin is linked/sharing-is-lawful: the same value, spelled with the hash listed ONCE and referenced twice. The pair is what pins first-use order as deduplicating: this spelling is what an encoder produces if it appends per REFERENCE instead of per DISTINCT CHILD.
pins: 3. The same hash MUST NOT appear twice: `duplicate_link_hash`.

invalid_cases.name: invalid/links-out-of-order
invalid_cases.clause: §6 — each distinct child hash is appended at the moment it is FIRST REFERENCED, scanning the body in canonical key order.
invalid_cases.note: ⭐ THESE ARE EXACTLY THE OCTETS batch 1 published as `linked/first-use-order`'s counterfactual address, and the digest here is that same 5567e8a3… — recomputed, matching. So the lawful twin and its refusal are now ONE artifact pair rather than a case and a number in a note. Scanning in key order gives 61 first, so first-use order is [chunk/leaf-01, chunk/leaf-02]; this header lists them reversed, which is what a core produces if it SORTS the header by hash. ⚠ The link indices are RENUMBERED to match (61→1, 63→0), so this spelling denotes THE SAME VALUE as the lawful case — that is what makes it a counterfactual rather than a different tree, and batch 1 records the naive non-renumbered variant (740c856e…) as the trap.
pins: 6. The header order MUST equal first-use order: otherwise `links_out_of_order`.

invalid_cases.name: invalid/leaf-codec-mismatch

child_chunk.note: Byte-identical to chunk/leaf-01 EXCEPT its id is 0002 (ontos-codec-v1) where the parent's is 0001. That one octet is the whole fault.

invalid_cases.clause: §4 — one artifact, one leaf codec: every chunk of one linked closure carries the same id, and a child whose id differs from its parent's MUST be refused.
invalid_cases.note: ⛔ UNREACHABLE IN THE FLAT FORM, which is why it appears only here: a flat artifact names its id exactly ONCE, in its header, so there is no second id to disagree with. ⚠ And it is invisible to anyone holding ONE chunk — parent and child are each individually well formed, and the fault is a RELATION between two headers. That is what makes `links` the right locus even though the differing octet sits in a header: the observational position that can see it is the one that holds the closure.
